lesson.title: Generate values with clear boundaries

steps.headline: arange steps by a size and stops before its stop, while linspace fixes how many points and includes both ends.

lead.text: np.arange(2, 12, 3) starts at 2, adds 3 each time, and stops before 12. np.linspace(2, 14, 5) gives exactly 5 evenly spaced points, including both 2 and 14.
arange excludes its stop. linspace includes its endpoint by default.
Start at the first value, add the step, and stop before you reach the stop value.

reveal.text: You listed the values before the stop. The stop itself was excluded, which is why arange can fall short of it.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(5)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(2, 12, 3)

steps.headline: What are the spacing and the values of np.linspace(0, 10, 6)?

workedSteps.text: Six points that include both ends have one fewer gap than points.
The span is shared among the gaps.
Step from the start by that spacing.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4, endpoint=False)

steps.headline: For np.linspace(2, 14, 5), what are the spacing and the final value?

workedSteps.text: Five points make four gaps across the span 14 − 2. What is the spacing?
The endpoint is included by default. What is the final value?

steps.headline: rng.integers(low, high) includes low and excludes high, and a seed makes the draws repeatable.

lead.text: np.random.default_rng(21) makes a generator. Giving it the same seed makes it produce the same sequence again. rng.integers(low, high) can return low but never high.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(22)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

lead.text: rng.integers excludes its upper bound, so every value it returns lies below that bound.

reveal.text: The high bound never appears, so the largest result sits one below it. That is the same stop-excluded rule as arange.

lead.text: Two generators are made with the same seed, and each draws the same four integers. The same seed and the same operations give the same sequence.

reveal.text: Matching seeds gave matching draws. That makes your work repeatable, but it does not make the sample representative of anything.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
b = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
b = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

lesson.orientation: Distinguish arange, linspace and reproducible random draws.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A path is 15 metres long. You put a post at the start, a post at the end, and a post every 3 metres in between.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell where arange stops and linspace ends, count the values each makes, and say what a random seed does.

recap.keyIdea: arange stops before its stop and linspace includes its endpoint; integers excludes its high bound, and a seed repeats a sequence without making it representative.

blocks.text: You put 6 posts along the path. You found np.arange(3, 15, 3) holds 4 values, and that two generators with one seed differ in 0 positions.

recap.nextHook: Next: meet a real table and read it into pandas.

questions.prompt: How many values are in np.arange(3, 15, 3)?
hints: List the values before the stop.
Start with the first value and add the step each time.
Count the values strictly below the stop.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The values are 3, 6, 9 and 12. The stop is excluded.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The values are 3, 6, 9 and 12. The next one would reach the stop, and the stop is excluded.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the stop value. arange never includes it.
Keep stepping while the value is still below the stop.

questions.prompt: What is the final value of np.linspace(2, 14, 5)?
hints: The third argument is the number of points.
The endpoint setting was not changed.
The stop is the final point.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: linspace includes the endpoint by default, so the final value is 14.

questions.onCorrect: 14. linspace includes the endpoint by default, so the stop is the last value.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value one spacing before the end. The endpoint itself is included.

questions.prompt: Which call generates integers from 1 through 6 with the default endpoint setting?
hints: Make high one larger than the largest outcome.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The lower bound is included and the upper bound excluded, so the range 1 to 7 contains 1 through 6.

questions.onCorrect: rng.integers(1, 7). The low bound is included and the high bound is excluded.

misconceptions.feedback: That can never return 6, because the high bound is excluded.

questions.prompt: Two generators use the same seed and each draws four integers. In how many positions do their results differ?
hints: Does the same seed start the sequence in the same place?
The same operations are repeated.
Count the positions where the two results disagree.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal seeds and equal operations give equal draws.

questions.onCorrect: 0. The same seed and the same operations give the same sequence. That is repeatability, not representativeness.

misconceptions.feedback: A seed makes the sequence repeat, so the results match.

questions.prompt: How many possible integer outcomes does rng.integers(4, 9) allow?
hints: Count the integers in the half-open range.
The low bound is included and the high bound is excluded.
Count the integers starting at the low bound and stopping before the high one.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the high bound. It is excluded.
That is the span. Count the integers from the low bound up to just below the high one.

questions.prompt: What is the spacing in np.linspace(0, 15, 6)?
hints: Six points that include both ends make one fewer gap.
The span is the stop minus the start.
Share the span among the gaps.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six points including both ends create five equal gaps: 15 ÷ 5 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Six points make five gaps, and the span of 15 is shared among them.

misconceptions.feedback: That shares the span among six gaps. Six points make five gaps.

hints: Start at 0 and add the step each time.
The stop value is excluded.
List the values below 1 and count them.
questions.prompt: How many values are in np.arange(0, 1, 0.25)?
questions.onCorrect: 4. The values are 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. The next one would reach the stop.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes 1, the stop value. arange excludes it.
The start value 0 is included too.

hints: Posts stand at 0, 3 and so on.
There is a post at both ends of the path.
Count the posts from 0 up to and including 15.
questions.prompt: How many posts are there altogether?
questions.onCorrect: 6. Posts at 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15. Counting both ends is what linspace does, and arange does not.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the gaps between posts. There is one more post than there are gaps.
That stops before 15. Both ends of the path have a post.

hints: One of them is defined by a number of points, not a step.
questions.prompt: Which call includes its stop value by default?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: linspace includes its endpoint by default; arange excludes its stop.

questions.onCorrect: linspace. It spreads points from the start to the stop, so the endpoint is included. arange stops before it.

misconceptions.feedback: arange stops before its stop value.
Only linspace includes its endpoint by default.

hints: Picture six fence posts in a line. How many gaps lie between them?
questions.prompt: Why are there only five gaps for six points?

choices.label: Both ends are points, so there is one fewer gap than points

acceptedIdeas: Both ends are points, so there is one fewer gap than points

questions.onCorrect: Both ends are points, so there is one fewer gap than there are points.

misconceptions.feedback: The number of gaps follows from the number of points you ask for.
No point is skipped. The gaps lie between neighbouring points.

hints: Five points make one fewer gap.
The span is the stop minus the start.
Share the span among the gaps.
questions.onCorrect: 3. The span of 12 is shared among four gaps.

misconceptions.feedback: That shares the span among five gaps. Five points make four gaps.

hints: Is the high bound included?
The values run from low up to just below high.
Which integer is just below 4?
questions.prompt: What is the largest value rng.integers(0, 4) can return?
questions.onCorrect: 3. The high bound is excluded, so the possible values are 0, 1, 2 and 3.

misconceptions.feedback: The high bound is excluded, so 4 never appears.
